questions.prompt: An 8-byte payload in the lesson's layout (13 bytes per frame, no stuffing) is sent at 100 Hz on a 57600 baud 8N1 link. Link load as a fraction, precision 0.001.
A telemetry frame carries 24 payload bytes (SOF, LEN, ID, SEQ, payload, CRC8). How many bytes is the frame before stuffing?
At most how many 11-byte frames per second fit on a 115200 baud 8N1 link at 100 % load? Precision 1.
An ATmega328P at 16 MHz uses double-speed mode (B = f/(8(UBRR+1))) with UBRR = 16. By how many percent does the actual baud rate differ from 115200? Give the signed value, precision 0.05.
CRC-8 (polynomial 0x07, init 0, no reflection) of the single byte 0x03, as a decimal number.
questions.explanation: CRC is linear over XOR: crc(0x03) = crc(0x01) xor crc(0x02) = 0x07 xor 0x0E = 0x09 = 9.

questions.prompt: Which error does a CRC8 over the frame detect that a plain one-byte sum of the same bytes does not?
options: A single flipped bit.
Two payload bytes swapped.
A payload shorter than the LEN field says.
A missing start byte.
questions.explanation: Swapping two bytes leaves the sum unchanged, but the CRC depends on the position of each byte. A flipped bit is caught by both.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does the data 7E 7D 00 7E take after byte stuffing (7E and 7D become two bytes each)?
The parser is collecting a frame and a bare 0x7E arrives. What should it do?
options: Treat it as payload data and keep waiting until LEN more bytes have arrived.
Reset the whole microcontroller, because a bare 0x7E proves that the link is corrupt.
Verify the CRC of the partial frame and then send an error reply to the host.
Count a truncated frame, drop the partial bytes and start a new frame.
questions.explanation: After stuffing, a bare 0x7E can only be a start marker. The partial frame is lost; the parser restarts without any explicit reset.

questions.prompt: Why must the parser reject a LEN byte above the maximum payload size immediately?
options: Otherwise one garbage byte makes it wait for bytes that never come and swallow good frames.
Because the CRC cannot be computed on frames longer than a few bytes at all.
Because the UART hardware silently drops any frame longer than 64 bytes.
Because LEN must always be equal to the sequence number of the frame.
questions.explanation: A garbage byte read as LEN = 200 would make the state machine wait for 204 bytes, swallowing the next valid frames. Checking LEN against the maximum keeps the resync fast.

questions.prompt: Consecutive good frames have sequence numbers 100 and 105. How many frames were lost?
Sequence numbers 254 then 1 arrive (8-bit counter). How many frames were lost?
A robot drives at 0.8 m/s and the MCU watchdog timeout is 250 ms. How far (in cm) can it travel after the host goes silent, ignoring braking distance?
The host sends commands at 50 Hz. Which MCU watchdog timeout is the most sensible default?
options: 20 ms, a single period, so the robot stops as fast as possible after any glitch.
About 60 to 100 ms, a few periods, so one late frame does not stop the robot.
2 minutes, so the robot never stops by accident while the operator looks away.
No timeout is needed because the CRC already protects the link against any problem.
questions.explanation: The timeout should span several command periods so one late or lost frame does not stop the robot, but remain short so the distance covered after link loss is small.

questions.prompt: Why is an Arduino Uno (ATmega328P, 2 kB SRAM) not a micro-ROS target while an ESP32 (520 kB RAM) is?
options: micro-ROS needs a 32-bit MCU with tens of kilobytes of RAM for the rcl/rclc stack and buffers.
micro-ROS only works over Wi-Fi or Ethernet transports, and the Uno has neither on its own board.
The Uno cannot generate PWM, and micro-ROS needs PWM output to talk to the agent at all.
micro-ROS requires a full Linux operating system on the microcontroller, which only the ESP32 can run.
questions.explanation: The Vulcanexus documentation states the main targets are mid-range 32-bit MCUs with tens of kilobytes of RAM. micro-ROS also runs over serial, so Wi-Fi is not required, and it runs on RTOSes or Arduino for supported boards.

questions.prompt: On the PC you run `ros2 topic list` while an ESP32 micro-ROS node publishes. What is true?
options: The MCU topic stays invisible until you install a vendor driver for the ESP32 on the PC side.
The topic appears like any other, because the micro-ROS agent created the DDS entities.
Only `ros2 topic echo` works; `ros2 topic list` cannot see topics coming from microcontrollers.
The topic appears only when the PC runs Windows, because Linux has no micro-ROS support yet.
questions.explanation: The agent represents the client in the DDS network, so standard tools see the topic. If the agent is not running, there is nothing on the PC side.

questions.prompt: A 12-motor quadruped needs 500 Hz joint control with bounded latency. Which link is the best fit?
options: A hobby USB-serial adapter with a text protocol and a high baud rate.
Wi-Fi UDP from the controller to each of the twelve motors.
micro-ROS over USB with DDS topics inside the 500 Hz loop.
CAN or EtherCAT drivers with bounded cycle times.
questions.explanation: USB-serial adapters batch data and have no bounded latency, Wi-Fi is not deterministic, and DDS in a 500 Hz loop adds jitter. CAN or EtherCAT give bounded timing.

questions.prompt: Write a test plan for a firmware frame parser that proves it resynchronises: list the damaged streams you feed, the expected delivered frames and the counters you check.
rubric: Feeds a clean frame as the baseline and the same stream one byte at a time.
Injects garbage before a frame, a flipped bit (CRC error), a truncated frame followed by a valid one, an oversized LEN and a payload containing 7E and 7D.
States the expected frames and counters (crc_errors, truncated, bad_length, lost) for each case and says what result would reject the parser.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Compare a custom serial protocol with a ros2_control hardware interface against micro-ROS for a 2-wheel robot, and say which you would use for a 6-joint arm with smart servos.
rubric: Custom serial plus a hardware interface: compact, deterministic read/write cycle, but you write and test the protocol and the plugin.
micro-ROS: a ready ROS 2 client and agent, sensors as topics, but more RAM and flash, an agent that must run and reconnect, and not suitable for a fast loop through DDS.
Arm with smart servos: use the servo bus through an existing driver or hardware interface rather than a new protocol, and keep timing-critical loops off USB-serial and DDS.
